claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 is in a hierarchical-heterostructured state with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
Integrating multiscale physics-informed descriptors with a tailored machine-learning model will enable rapid prediction of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness.

The hybrid model will predict the specified properties more accurately than standalone CALPHAD, first-principles calculations, and machine-learning models lacking integrated microstructural descriptors.
High-resolution electron microscopy and chemical mapping can provide quantitative descriptors of the alloy’s heterogeneities.
The hierarchical heterostructure and chemical-fluctuation patterns mediate the relationship between compositional state and mechanical performance.
Physics-informed descriptors reduce model input complexity.
Reducing input complexity permits interpolation across the design space using fewer computational resources.
Encoding microstructure–mechanics relationships constrains the machine-learning model and improves predictive accuracy.
The hybrid model will reduce prediction errors for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness by approximately 30–50% relative to the stated baselines.
The hybrid model will decrease computational demand by as much as one order of magnitude.
Predictions will be within ±10% of measured values for at least 80% of evaluated specimens.
Model reliability may fail when hierarchical microstructures deviate substantially from the training distribution.
Model reliability may fail under high-temperature creep or impact-loading conditions outside the proposed tensile and fracture-test regime.
Descriptor resolution and spatial representativeness may be inadequate across some mechanically relevant length scales.
Unmodeled microstructural variations may degrade predictions outside the training domain.
A blinded, independently tested set of HfNbTiVAl10 specimens can prospectively compare model predictions with standardized mechanical-test outcomes.
